arrow-crab.name: Yellowline arrow crab
arrow-crab.description: A spider of a crab, all legs and a needle nose, walking the reef at night.
arrow-crab.tip: Sweep a light slowly across a sponge face; the legs catch the beam first.

atlantic-spadefish.name: Atlantic spadefish
atlantic-spadefish.description: Tall silver discs banded in black, drifting over a wreck in a slow crowd.
atlantic-spadefish.tip: They circle rather than flee. Stay low and the whole school will come around again.

azure-vase-sponge.name: Azure vase sponge
azure-vase-sponge.description: A fluted violet-pink cup that almost glows against the reef face.
azure-vase-sponge.tip: Get low and shoot up into the cup — the colour only reads with light in it.

balloonfish.name: Balloonfish
balloonfish.description: A spiny puffer with long spines and copper eyes, resting under a ledge by day.
balloonfish.tip: Never provoke one into inflating — it is a stress response, not a trick.

banded-butterflyfish.name: Banded butterflyfish
banded-butterflyfish.description: A white disc crossed by four dark bands, almost always in a pair.
banded-butterflyfish.tip: Watch one pair for a minute — they work a patch of reef together and circle back.

banded-coral-shrimp.name: Banded coral shrimp
banded-coral-shrimp.description: Red-and-white candy stripes with white antennae twice its own length.
banded-coral-shrimp.tip: The waving antennae are the advertisement — look for those, not the body.

bandtail-puffer.name: Bandtail puffer
bandtail-puffer.description: A small mottled puffer with a row of dark blotches along the belly, low on the sand.
bandtail-puffer.tip: Sits still on the bottom and lets you pass. Sweep the sand at the reef edge for it.

bar-jack.name: Bar jack
bar-jack.description: A silver jack with one electric-blue stripe down the back, often shadowing a ray.
bar-jack.tip: When you find a stingray feeding, look just above it — a jack is usually riding along.

barred-hamlet.name: Barred hamlet
barred-hamlet.description: A small tan bass with a dark saddle amidships, hanging just off the coral.
barred-hamlet.tip: Hamlets hold a spot and watch you — approach one slowly instead of sweeping the reef.

black-coral.name: Black coral
black-coral.description: Feathery grey-green bushes on deep walls; the black is the skeleton inside.
black-coral.tip: Slow-growing and protected nearly everywhere. Keep fins and gauges well off the wall.

black-durgon.name: Black durgon
black-durgon.description: Black at a glance, and blue-green with bright seams once light reaches it.
black-durgon.tip: Put a light on one. The colour it looks at ten metres is not the colour it is.

black-grouper.name: Black grouper
black-grouper.description: A big, dark, rectangular grouper that holds station off the reef edge.
black-grouper.tip: Keep your distance and it stays; swim straight at it and the dive is over.

blackbar-soldierfish.name: Blackbar soldierfish
blackbar-soldierfish.description: Red, big-eyed and nocturnal, hanging upside-down inside caves by day.
blackbar-soldierfish.tip: Bring a light into an overhang and look at the ceiling, not the floor.

blue-chromis.name: Blue chromis
blue-chromis.description: Small electric-blue slivers hanging in open water just above the coral.
blue-chromis.tip: Look up and out from the reef rather than down; they feed in the water column.

blue-tang.name: Blue tang
blue-tang.description: A deep blue oval with a bright scalpel at the tail; juveniles are yellow.
blue-tang.tip: Hover rather than chase — a loose group grazes past you on its own.

bluehead-wrasse.name: Bluehead wrasse
bluehead-wrasse.description: Yellow youngsters and blue-headed adults, darting nose-down over the coral.
bluehead-wrasse.tip: Find a cleaning station and stay still; they come to you.

bluestriped-grunt.name: Bluestriped grunt
bluestriped-grunt.description: Yellow flanks ruled with electric blue lines, in loose crowds under ledges.
bluestriped-grunt.tip: Look into the shade under overhangs — a whole school can sit out the day there.

bottlenose-dolphin.name: Bottlenose dolphin
bottlenose-dolphin.description: Usually a surface encounter from the boat, occasionally a pass underwater.
bottlenose-dolphin.tip: Never chase. Stay where you are, and they decide whether it's a meeting.

boulder-star-coral.name: Boulder star coral
boulder-star-coral.description: Stacked columns with rounded tops, one of the reef's main frame-builders.
boulder-star-coral.tip: Much of the reef you are swimming over is this. It took centuries to reach that size.

branching-vase-sponge.name: Branching vase sponge
branching-vase-sponge.description: Clusters of purple-grey tubes with rough walls, leaning away from the current.
branching-vase-sponge.tip: Look into the tubes — brittle stars and small gobies live down inside them.

brown-chromis.name: Brown chromis
brown-chromis.description: Olive-brown slivers feeding in open water, often mixed in with the blue ones.
brown-chromis.tip: Where you find blue chromis, look again — the brown ones feed in the same cloud.

caribbean-reef-octopus.name: Caribbean reef octopus
caribbean-reef-octopus.description: Blue-green and shape-shifting, out hunting across the reef after dark.
caribbean-reef-octopus.tip: A night dive doubles your odds. Keep the light off its eyes and it stays out.

caribbean-reef-shark.name: Caribbean reef shark
caribbean-reef-shark.description: A classic grey requiem shark that patrols the reef edge in open water.
caribbean-reef-shark.tip: Stay off the bottom, keep the group together, and watch it rather than follow it.

caribbean-reef-squid.name: Caribbean reef squid
caribbean-reef-squid.description: A small squadron holding formation in mid-water, colours running across them.
caribbean-reef-squid.tip: Approach slowly and they hold. They are talking to each other in those colours.

chain-moray.name: Chain moray
chain-moray.description: Dark brown printed with a yellow chain-link pattern, and short for a moray.
chain-moray.tip: Hunts crabs in the shallows by day, sometimes half out of the water. Look shallow.

channel-clinging-crab.name: Channel clinging crab
channel-clinging-crab.description: A dinner-plate crab wedged into a crevice, out only when the lights go down.
channel-clinging-crab.tip: Check the deep cracks in a wall — you see the claws before the animal.

christmas-tree-worm.name: Christmas tree worm
christmas-tree-worm.description: Pairs of tiny coloured spirals growing straight out of hard coral.
christmas-tree-worm.tip: Wave a hand near one and every worm on the head vanishes at once. Then wait.

cobia.name: Cobia
cobia.description: A dark torpedo often mistaken for a shark, cruising past wrecks in open water.
cobia.tip: Look into the blue away from the structure, not only along it.

common-sea-fan.name: Common sea fan
common-sea-fan.description: A purple lattice standing across the current like a window frame.
common-sea-fan.tip: They grow square to the prevailing current — a useful natural compass.

coney.name: Coney
coney.description: A hand-length grouper that comes in red, brown or bright yellow, all one species.
coney.tip: Tucked into sponges and ledges. The yellow phase is the one people photograph.

corkscrew-anemone.name: Corkscrew anemone
corkscrew-anemone.description: Long tentacles ringed with pale spirals, always with something living in them.
corkscrew-anemone.tip: Check inside every one. Cleaner shrimp and juvenile fish shelter there in the day.

creole-wrasse.name: Creole wrasse
creole-wrasse.description: Violet fish streaming along the reef edge in long, fast trains.
creole-wrasse.tip: Hold position at the drop-off and let the train come past you.

cubera-snapper.name: Cubera snapper
cubera-snapper.description: The biggest Caribbean snapper — heavy-jawed, grey, and usually alone on a wreck.
cubera-snapper.tip: Solitary and wary. If one lets you close, stop where you are rather than pressing on.

cushion-sea-star.name: Cushion sea star
cushion-sea-star.description: A fat orange star the size of a dinner plate, out on open sand and seagrass.
cushion-sea-star.tip: Leave it in the water. Lifting one for a photo is what kills them.

dog-snapper.name: Dog snapper
dog-snapper.description: Bronze, with a pale triangle under the eye and two canines it is named for.
dog-snapper.tip: Holds station at the mouth of a swim-through. Look before you enter, not after.

donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.name: Donkey dung sea cucumber
donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.description: A heavy brown cucumber lying on open sand, processing it a mouthful at a time.
donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.tip: Leave it be. Handling one makes it shed its insides, which it may not survive.

elkhorn-coral.name: Elkhorn coral
elkhorn-coral.description: Broad antler branches in the shallows, the classic Caribbean reef silhouette.
elkhorn-coral.tip: This is the shallowest part of most dives — watch your fins above it.

feather-duster-worm.name: Magnificent feather duster
feather-duster-worm.description: A soft banded fan on a tube, retracting the instant a shadow crosses it.
feather-duster-worm.tip: Approach from downstream and stay out of its light; it feels you coming.

finger-coral.name: Finger coral
finger-coral.description: Stubby blunt fingers in low thickets, tan to pale purple, in shallow water.
finger-coral.tip: A nursery: look between the fingers for the smallest fish on the reef.

fire-coral.name: Branching fire coral
fire-coral.description: Mustard-tan blades with pale tips, growing over anything that stops moving.
fire-coral.tip: Not a coral and it does sting. Learn the mustard colour and keep clear.

flamingo-tongue.name: Flamingo tongue
flamingo-tongue.description: A thumbnail snail wrapped in orange leopard print, grazing on sea fans.
flamingo-tongue.tip: Search the sea fans, not the coral. The pattern is living tissue, not the shell.

foureye-butterflyfish.name: Foureye butterflyfish
foureye-butterflyfish.description: A pale disc with one big false eyespot near the tail, to send a predator the wrong way.
foureye-butterflyfish.tip: Approach from the side; head-on they turn and show you the fake eye.

french-angelfish.name: French angelfish
french-angelfish.description: A tall, dark disc scaled in tiny yellow crescents, usually in pairs.
french-angelfish.tip: Stay still for a moment beside a sponge and the pair often comes to look at you.

french-grunt.name: French grunt
french-grunt.description: Yellow-striped fish stacked in the hundreds around coral heads.
french-grunt.tip: Move slowly into the school and it will part and reform around you.

garden-eel.name: Garden eel
garden-eel.description: A field of pencil-thin eels standing out of the sand, swaying into the current.
garden-eel.tip: They vanish as you approach. Settle at a distance, wait, and the whole field grows back.

giant-anemone.name: Giant Caribbean anemone
giant-anemone.description: A bouquet of purple- or pink-tipped tentacles, often with a shrimp living in it.
giant-anemone.tip: Look inside before you move on — the cleaner shrimp are the real find.

giant-barrel-sponge.name: Giant barrel sponge
giant-barrel-sponge.description: A rust-coloured barrel wide enough to climb into, and centuries old.
giant-barrel-sponge.tip: Never rest a hand on the rim. Some of these were here before Florida was a state.

giant-basket-star.name: Giant basket star
giant-basket-star.description: A tangle of branching arms that opens into a feeding net after dark.
giant-basket-star.tip: By day it is a knot on a sea rod. Come back at night to see it open.

glasseye-snapper.name: Glasseye snapper
glasseye-snapper.description: Red and silver with an enormous eye, hanging head-down in a shaded hollow.
glasseye-snapper.tip: A night feeder resting by day. Any dark recess at eye level is worth a second look.

glassy-sweeper.name: Glassy sweeper
glassy-sweeper.description: Copper-coloured clouds that fill the shaded spaces inside a wreck or ledge.
glassy-sweeper.tip: Stay outside the structure and let the school reform around you.

goldentail-moray.name: Goldentail moray
goldentail-moray.description: Dark brown flecked with gold, small enough to live in a fist-sized hole.
goldentail-moray.tip: Scan holes at chest height on the reef face, not just at the base.

goliath-grouper.name: Goliath grouper
goliath-grouper.description: Enormous and unbothered — usually parked under a ledge or in a wreck's shadow.
goliath-grouper.tip: Give it room and never block its way out from under an overhang.

gray-angelfish.name: Gray angelfish
gray-angelfish.description: The French angelfish's larger, plainer cousin, with a pale square-cut tail.
gray-angelfish.tip: Tell it from a French angelfish by the tail — square and light, not round and dark.

gray-snapper.name: Gray snapper
gray-snapper.description: Wary grey-red snapper that hang in the lee of wrecks and mangrove roots.
gray-snapper.tip: They watch you first — approach at an angle rather than head-on and they hold.

graysby.name: Graysby
graysby.description: A small pale grouper freckled all over, with four dots along the top of the back.
graysby.tip: Count the four dots on the dorsal ridge — that is the tell against every other small grouper.

great-barracuda.name: Great barracuda
great-barracuda.description: A long silver bar with an underslung jaw, hanging motionless in the current.
great-barracuda.tip: It is curious, not interested in you — leave shiny gear tucked away and carry on.

great-star-coral.name: Great star coral
great-star-coral.description: Boulders studded with fat, evenly spaced cups that open and feed at night.
great-star-coral.tip: Come back with a light after dark — the whole boulder is in bloom.

green-moray.name: Green moray
green-moray.description: A heavy olive eel that fills a crevice and breathes with its mouth open.
green-moray.tip: The open mouth is breathing, not a threat — keep hands away and it stays calm.

green-sea-turtle.name: Green sea turtle
green-sea-turtle.description: A smooth-shelled grazer, usually head-down in seagrass or asleep under a ledge.
green-sea-turtle.tip: Stay off its path to the surface — it has to breathe, and it will not go around you.

grooved-brain-coral.name: Grooved brain coral
grooved-brain-coral.description: A rounded head patterned with maze-like ridges and deep valleys.
grooved-brain-coral.tip: Notice the pattern while keeping fins and hands safely clear.

hawksbill-turtle.name: Hawksbill turtle
hawksbill-turtle.description: A narrow beak and a serrated shell edge, picking sponges off the reef face.
hawksbill-turtle.tip: The beak is the tell: pointed and hooked, where a green turtle's is blunt.

hogfish.name: Hogfish
hogfish.description: A long-snouted wrasse that roots through sand and rubble for shellfish.
hogfish.tip: Follow the puffs of sand — it makes the mess before you spot the fish.

honeycomb-cowfish.name: Honeycomb cowfish
honeycomb-cowfish.description: A boxy fish tiled in hexagons, with two small horns over the eyes.
honeycomb-cowfish.tip: Look low over the sand between coral heads; it hovers rather than swims.

horse-eye-jack.name: Horse-eye jack
horse-eye-jack.description: Big-eyed silver jacks that roll past in tight, fast schools.
horse-eye-jack.tip: Watch the blue over the wreck for a wall of them rather than scanning the deck.

indigo-hamlet.name: Indigo hamlet
indigo-hamlet.description: Deep blue banded with white, and one of the harder Caribbean fish to find.
indigo-hamlet.tip: Worth the whole dive if you get one. Try the deeper coral heads, not the shallows.

lemon-shark.name: Lemon shark
lemon-shark.description: Yellow-brown, blunt-nosed, with two dorsal fins nearly the same size.
lemon-shark.tip: Common over sand flats and in shallow channels — look away from the coral.

lettuce-coral.name: Lettuce coral
lettuce-coral.description: Thin ruffled plates growing in overlapping layers down the shaded side of a slope.
lettuce-coral.tip: Grows where the light is poor, so look under and behind rather than on top.

lettuce-sea-slug.name: Lettuce sea slug
lettuce-sea-slug.description: Ruffled green frills on a slug the size of a coin, grazing on rock and rubble.
lettuce-sea-slug.tip: It keeps the algae's chloroplasts alive inside itself and feeds on sunlight. Look in the shallows.

lionfish.name: Lionfish
lionfish.description: Striped fans of venomous spines — beautiful, and not from this ocean.
lionfish.tip: Invasive here. Admire it, keep well clear of the spines, and report it to the crew.

loggerhead-turtle.name: Loggerhead turtle
loggerhead-turtle.description: A heavy reddish head built for crushing conch and lobster.
loggerhead-turtle.tip: Give a feeding loggerhead a wide berth — that jaw is doing serious work.

long-spined-urchin.name: Long-spined sea urchin
long-spined-urchin.description: A black pincushion with spines as long as your hand; the reef's best grazer.
long-spined-urchin.tip: Mind your knees and fins in a swim-through. The spines break off in you.

longlure-frogfish.name: Longlure frogfish
longlure-frogfish.description: A lumpy sponge that turns out to have a mouth, fishing with a lure on its head.
longlure-frogfish.tip: Guides find these and divers do not. If your guide stops at bare sponge, look harder.

longsnout-butterflyfish.name: Longsnout butterflyfish
longsnout-butterflyfish.description: Small, yellow-backed and long-faced, working the shaded parts of a wall.
longsnout-butterflyfish.tip: A wall fish rather than a reef-flat one — look under overhangs on the way back up.

longsnout-seahorse.name: Longsnout seahorse
longsnout-seahorse.description: A seahorse the length of a finger, anchored by its tail to a sponge or a rope.
longsnout-seahorse.tip: Never move one for a photograph, and keep the light off it — bright light stresses them.

mahogany-snapper.name: Mahogany snapper
mahogany-snapper.description: Silver with red-edged fins and a big eye, in loose crowds over the coral by day.
mahogany-snapper.tip: Drifts rather than schools tightly. Move through the group slowly and it barely reacts.

manatee.name: West Indian manatee
manatee.description: A grey, slow, whiskered grazer of warm springs and inshore channels.
manatee.tip: Protected: passive observation only. Hands off, no pursuit, no blocking its route.

maze-coral.name: Maze coral
maze-coral.description: Wide, deep valleys running in long curves — a brain coral drawn with a bigger pen.
maze-coral.tip: Tell it from a brain coral by the valleys: fewer, wider, and running further before they turn.

midnight-parrotfish.name: Midnight parrotfish
midnight-parrotfish.description: Deep blue-black all over, with a brighter blue beak; big and easy to miss.
midnight-parrotfish.tip: It reads as a dark shape against dark coral. Look for the beak, not the body.

moon-jelly.name: Moon jelly
moon-jelly.description: A translucent saucer with four horseshoe rings, pulsing through open water.
moon-jelly.tip: Mild sting at worst, but a hood and gloves make a swarm a pleasure instead of a chore.

mountainous-star-coral.name: Mountainous star coral
mountainous-star-coral.description: Great mounded sheets with a fine even texture, the biggest heads on many reefs.
mountainous-star-coral.tip: Pale patches are bleaching, not a pattern. Worth reporting to the crew if you see a lot.

mustard-hill-coral.name: Mustard hill coral
mustard-hill-coral.description: Low mustard-yellow domes with a bumpy surface, common in the shallows.
mustard-hill-coral.tip: One of the few corals doing well right now — you will see it on almost every dive.

mutton-snapper.name: Mutton snapper
mutton-snapper.description: Olive above and rose below, with a small black spot high on the flank.
mutton-snapper.tip: Hunts over sand at the reef edge — look away from the coral rather than into it.

nassau-grouper.name: Nassau grouper
nassau-grouper.description: Banded brown and cream with a dark saddle at the tail, and famously curious.
nassau-grouper.tip: Protected and slow to recover — look, photograph, and leave it where it is.

nurse-shark.name: Nurse shark
nurse-shark.description: A broad, mellow bottom-rester with rounded fins and two barbels at the snout.
nurse-shark.tip: Check quiet ledges without crowding or blocking an animal's way out.

ocean-triggerfish.name: Ocean triggerfish
ocean-triggerfish.description: A tall grey diamond with a dark blotch at the pectoral, out in the blue off a wall.
ocean-triggerfish.tip: Look off the wall rather than along it — this one hangs in open water, not on the reef.

orange-elephant-ear-sponge.name: Orange elephant ear sponge
orange-elephant-ear-sponge.description: Broad orange sheets folded out from a wall, the brightest thing at depth.
orange-elephant-ear-sponge.tip: Hawksbill turtles eat these — a chewed edge means one has been through recently.

peacock-flounder.name: Peacock flounder
peacock-flounder.description: A flat sand-coloured disc with blue rings, both eyes on one side.
peacock-flounder.tip: It only becomes visible when it moves — sweep the sand, don't stare at it.

pederson-cleaner-shrimp.name: Pederson cleaner shrimp
pederson-cleaner-shrimp.description: A glass shrimp with violet spots, waving from inside an anemone.
pederson-cleaner-shrimp.tip: Hold a bare hand still near the anemone and it may well come and clean it.

permit-fish.name: Permit
permit-fish.description: A tall, mirror-flat silver disc that appears over wrecks and vanishes as fast.
permit-fish.tip: Keep the camera ready on the descent — permit meet you on the way down, not at depth.

pillar-coral.name: Pillar coral
pillar-coral.description: Furry-looking spires standing upright off the bottom; rare and getting rarer.
pillar-coral.tip: The fuzz is polyps out feeding by day — one of the few corals that does.

porcupinefish.name: Porcupinefish
porcupinefish.description: A big-eyed spiny balloon that wedges itself under a ledge to sleep.
porcupinefish.tip: Never provoke one into inflating — it is a stress response, not a trick.

porkfish.name: Porkfish
porkfish.description: Two black head bars and a yellow body — the tidiest fish on the reef.
porkfish.tip: Check the up-current side of a coral head, where they hold station together.

princess-parrotfish.name: Princess parrotfish
princess-parrotfish.description: Blue-green with two bright stripes along the face, grazing in small groups.
princess-parrotfish.tip: The stripes run through the eye — that is what separates it from a striped parrotfish.

queen-angelfish.name: Queen angelfish
queen-angelfish.description: Blue and gold with a ringed crown on the forehead and long trailing fins.
queen-angelfish.tip: Quiet breathing helps: it keeps a coral head between you and it if you rush.

queen-conch.name: Queen conch
queen-conch.description: A heavy flared shell on seagrass sand, dragging itself along on one foot.
queen-conch.tip: Protected in Florida. Look for the two stalked eyes, and put nothing in your pocket.

queen-parrotfish.name: Queen parrotfish
queen-parrotfish.description: Blue-green with bright bands running from the beak, grazing along the coral.
queen-parrotfish.tip: Follow the crunching sound; you will hear it working before you see it.

queen-triggerfish.name: Queen triggerfish
queen-triggerfish.description: Blue-lined and gaudy, swimming with a rippling pair of fins rather than its tail.
queen-triggerfish.tip: Nesting fish defend a cone of water above the nest — go around, not over.

rainbow-parrotfish.name: Rainbow parrotfish
rainbow-parrotfish.description: The biggest parrotfish in the Atlantic — bronze-green, and over a metre grown.
rainbow-parrotfish.tip: It grows up in the mangroves, so a reef beside one is where you have the best chance.

red-grouper.name: Red grouper
red-grouper.description: Rust-coloured, square-jawed, and dug into its own excavated hollow in the bottom.
red-grouper.tip: Look for a scooped pit in the sand or rubble — the fish is usually sitting in it.

red-rope-sponge.name: Erect rope sponge
red-rope-sponge.description: Deep red cords standing off the reef, stiff and slightly branched.
red-rope-sponge.tip: The red survives deeper than most colours — a useful marker on a wall.

redband-parrotfish.name: Redband parrotfish
redband-parrotfish.description: Small and mottled, with a pale patch behind the head and a red-edged tail.
redband-parrotfish.tip: The commonest parrotfish on most Caribbean reefs, and the one nobody stops to look at.

redlip-blenny.name: Redlip blenny
redlip-blenny.description: A dark, blunt-headed little fish propped on its fins in a hole in the coral.
redlip-blenny.tip: Shallow and territorial — check the same knob of coral twice and it will be back out.

reef-butterflyfish.name: Reef butterflyfish
reef-butterflyfish.description: Pale with a dark wash across the back half, always somewhere near its partner.
reef-butterflyfish.tip: Deeper than the other butterflyfish here — expect it below twenty metres, in pairs.

remora.name: Remora
remora.description: A striped rider that detaches from its host and circles whatever comes past.
remora.tip: If one takes an interest in you, just keep swimming — it loses interest.

rock-beauty.name: Rock beauty
rock-beauty.description: Yellow at both ends with a black saddle in the middle, never far from a hole.
rock-beauty.tip: Watch one gap in the reef rather than sweeping — it comes back out to the same spot.

rock-hind.name: Rock hind
rock-hind.description: A stocky grouper covered in red-brown spots, wedged into rubble or a wreck plate.
rock-hind.tip: Prefers broken ground to clean coral. Search the rubble field, not the reef top.

royal-gramma.name: Royal gramma
royal-gramma.description: Purple in front, gold behind, thumb-sized, and often swimming upside down.
royal-gramma.tip: Look into the roof of a small cave or under a ledge — it orients its belly to the rock.

sand-diver.name: Sand diver
sand-diver.description: A propped-up lizardfish that sits on the sand until something small swims by.
sand-diver.tip: Look for a stick shape with eyes at the edge of a sand channel.

schoolmaster-snapper.name: Schoolmaster snapper
schoolmaster-snapper.description: Yellow-finned snapper that hover in the shade of coral heads and wreck plates.
schoolmaster-snapper.tip: Look into the structure rather than over it; they hold just inside the shadow line.

scrawled-filefish.name: Scrawled filefish
scrawled-filefish.description: Olive with blue scribbles, drifting nose-down like a leaf in the current.
scrawled-filefish.tip: It hides by going vertical — check anything that looks like a piece of debris.

sea-plume.name: Sea plume
sea-plume.description: Feathery gorgonians that sway the whole reef in time with the swell.
sea-plume.tip: Watch them to read the surge before you commit to a swim-through.

sergeant-major.name: Sergeant major
sergeant-major.description: Small, striped and everywhere, guarding purple egg patches on hard surfaces.
sergeant-major.tip: A guarding male will bump your mask — back off rather than push in.

sharknose-goby.name: Sharknose goby
sharknose-goby.description: A tiny neon-striped goby that runs a cleaning station on top of a coral head.
sharknose-goby.tip: Find one and wait. Whatever queues up for its service is the rest of the reef arriving.

sharpnose-puffer.name: Sharpnose puffer
sharpnose-puffer.description: A thumb-sized puffer with blue-lined eyes, hovering nose-down over the coral.
sharpnose-puffer.tip: Everywhere once you know it, and the easiest small fish on the reef to get close to.

sharptail-eel.name: Sharptail eel
sharptail-eel.description: A pale spotted eel out in the open over sand and seagrass, nosing under rubble.
sharptail-eel.tip: Unlike a moray it travels in daylight. A moving eel in the open is almost always this.

slipper-lobster.name: Slipper lobster
slipper-lobster.description: A flattened, plate-like lobster with shovels for antennae, pressed into a crevice.
slipper-lobster.tip: It reads as a piece of the reef until it moves. Check the roof of a cave, not the floor.

smooth-trunkfish.name: Smooth trunkfish
smooth-trunkfish.description: A hovering box with pursed lips that blows sand away to find its food.
smooth-trunkfish.tip: Watch it puff at the sand — the whole feeding trick happens in a few seconds.

southern-stingray.name: Southern stingray
southern-stingray.description: A grey diamond gliding over the sand, or buried with only its eyes showing.
southern-stingray.tip: Give rays space and watch from the side, not from above.

spanish-hogfish.name: Spanish hogfish
spanish-hogfish.description: Purple over gold; the young ones run cleaning stations for bigger fish.
spanish-hogfish.tip: Find a juvenile at work and you have found the reef's cleaning station.

spiny-lobster.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
spiny-lobster.description: No claws, but two long whips of antennae sticking out from under a ledge.
spiny-lobster.tip: The antennae give it away long before the body does. Check every dark gap.

splendid-toadfish.name: Splendid toadfish
splendid-toadfish.description: Flat-headed, white-striped, yellow-finned — and found nowhere on earth but Cozumel.
splendid-toadfish.tip: It sits far back under ledges. Light the gap without crowding it and it will hold.

spotfin-butterflyfish.name: Spotfin butterflyfish
spotfin-butterflyfish.description: White with a yellow trailing edge and a dark bar through the eye.
spotfin-butterflyfish.tip: Look along the reef's sandy edge at dusk, when pairs come out to feed.

spotted-cleaner-shrimp.name: Spotted cleaner shrimp
spotted-cleaner-shrimp.description: A glass shrimp saddled with white and purple, living inside a stinging anemone.
spotted-cleaner-shrimp.tip: It advertises by waving. Watch one work a fish and you have seen the reef's whole economy.

spotted-drum.name: Spotted drum
spotted-drum.description: Black-and-white, with an absurdly long first fin the juveniles wave like a ribbon.
spotted-drum.tip: Check the shaded floor of a swim-through; it circles the same small patch all day.

spotted-eagle-ray.name: Spotted eagle ray
spotted-eagle-ray.description: Black wings freckled with white, flying past in open water with a whip of a tail.
spotted-eagle-ray.tip: Look out into the blue at the start of the dive — they pass through, they don't stay.

spotted-moray.name: Spotted moray
spotted-moray.description: White peppered with dark spots, usually one head poking from the rubble.
spotted-moray.tip: Look into rubble and wreck gaps rather than the open reef face.

spotted-scorpionfish.name: Spotted scorpionfish
spotted-scorpionfish.description: Invisible until it moves — a lump of reef with venomous spines along its back.
spotted-scorpionfish.tip: This is why you never put a hand down to steady yourself. Look before you touch.

spotted-trunkfish.name: Spotted trunkfish
spotted-trunkfish.description: A white box covered in black dots, sculling along on two small fins.
spotted-trunkfish.tip: Its shell means it cannot bend, so it turns its whole body — a slow, comic swimmer.

squirrelfish.name: Squirrelfish
squirrelfish.description: Red and silver with huge night-adapted eyes, tucked into a hole by day.
squirrelfish.tip: Red goes grey at depth without a light — hold a torch on it to see the colour.

staghorn-coral.name: Staghorn coral
staghorn-coral.description: Dense thickets of finger-thick branches, and a nursery for everything small.
staghorn-coral.tip: Fragile and slow-growing. Keep your fins high; a kick takes years back.

stoplight-parrotfish.name: Stoplight parrotfish
stoplight-parrotfish.description: A heavy beaked grazer — green and gold as an adult, mottled red as a youngster.
stoplight-parrotfish.tip: Move slowly near coral heads and let the colour find you.

stovepipe-sponge.name: Stovepipe sponge
stovepipe-sponge.description: Long pale tubes standing well off the wall, tall enough to swim alongside.
stovepipe-sponge.tip: A wall species. On a drift these are the landmark you use to judge how fast you are going.

symmetrical-brain-coral.name: Symmetrical brain coral
symmetrical-brain-coral.description: Tighter, more even ridges than its grooved cousin, in flatter domes.
symmetrical-brain-coral.tip: The valleys hold tiny life — put a light in one instead of swimming past.

tarpon.name: Tarpon
tarpon.description: A slab of living chrome, up to two metres, hanging in a wreck's lee.
tarpon.tip: Cut your light on a night dive and let them work the edge of everyone else's.

threespot-damselfish.name: Threespot damselfish
threespot-damselfish.description: A small brown farmer with a black spot at the tail, guarding its patch of algae.
threespot-damselfish.tip: It will charge a diver ten times its size. That is a display, and it always stops.

tiger-grouper.name: Tiger grouper
tiger-grouper.description: Slanted tiger bars over a long body, very often parked at a cleaning station.
tiger-grouper.tip: Find the cleaning station and you find the grouper, mouth open and holding still.

trumpetfish.name: Trumpetfish
trumpetfish.description: A long tube of a fish that hangs head-down among sea rods, pretending to be one.
trumpetfish.tip: Scan vertical shapes in a soft-coral stand — it is hiding in plain sight.

turtle-grass.name: Turtle grass
turtle-grass.description: Ribbon meadows on the sand flats where the reef's next generation grows up.
turtle-grass.tip: Hover, don't stand. Every fin-print in a seagrass bed lasts for months.

upside-down-jellyfish.name: Upside-down jellyfish
upside-down-jellyfish.description: A jellyfish lying bell-down on the bottom, farming sunlight with its tentacles up.
upside-down-jellyfish.tip: Common in shallow, sheltered bays — don't kneel on one; they do sting.

whale-shark.name: Whale shark
whale-shark.description: A checkerboard the size of a bus, filter-feeding at the surface in season.
whale-shark.tip: Never touch or block its path, and stay clear of the tail. Local rules set the distance.

white-grunt.name: White grunt
white-grunt.description: Pale blue and yellow head lines, with a flash of orange inside the mouth.
white-grunt.tip: They really do grunt — you can hear a school through the water on a quiet dive.

yellow-stingray.name: Yellow stingray
yellow-stingray.description: A small, round, mottled ray that lies still in the sand between coral heads.
yellow-stingray.tip: Shuffle rather than kick down onto sand — this is the one most divers land on.

yellow-tube-sponge.name: Yellow tube sponge
yellow-tube-sponge.description: Clusters of yellow chimneys standing off the wall, each one an open pipe.
yellow-tube-sponge.tip: A reliable colour marker in poor visibility — you can see the yellow from far off.

yellowfin-grouper.name: Yellowfin grouper
yellowfin-grouper.description: Blotched red or grey with a yellow rim to the pectoral fins, out on the wall.
yellowfin-grouper.tip: The yellow fin edge is the only reliable mark — its body colour changes as you watch.

yellowhead-jawfish.name: Yellowhead jawfish
yellowhead-jawfish.description: A pale fish hovering upright over its burrow, dropping in tail-first when startled.
yellowhead-jawfish.tip: Settle on the sand at a distance and wait — it comes back up within a minute.

yellowhead-wrasse.name: Yellowhead wrasse
yellowhead-wrasse.description: Yellow-headed adults and lemon-yellow youngsters, never still for a moment.
yellowhead-wrasse.tip: Too fast to chase. Pick a coral head, hold, and let it work its way back around to you.

yellowtail-damselfish.name: Yellowtail damselfish
yellowtail-damselfish.description: Dark body, bright yellow tail; the young ones are speckled with electric blue.
yellowtail-damselfish.tip: The juveniles are the show — look for blue sparks over fire coral in the shallows.

yellowtail-snapper.name: Yellowtail snapper
yellowtail-snapper.description: Silver schools ruled by one bright yellow stripe running out into the tail.
yellowtail-snapper.tip: Look into the blue beyond the reef instead of only looking down.

spreadsheet.columnsTitle: Does your sheet have these columns?
spreadsheet.columnsIntro: One row per diver, saved as CSV. Your headings don't have to match anything — DiveDay recognizes the common names and flags what it doesn't.

name.detail: First and last in two columns, or one full-name column. The only thing a row truly needs.

email.detail: How DiveDay reaches a diver and recognizes a returning one, so a second import updates instead of duplicating. A row without one still comes in.

phone.detail: Mobile or landline, however you've written it.

emergencyContact.detail: A name and a phone number, when you have them, land on the diver's card.

diveInsurance.detail: A DAN number, a provider name — comes across as written. Never a gate; it's what the crew wants on hand in an incident.

certification.detail: Agency, level, and card number. The card number is what lets a card come across at all.

refresherDue.detail: Written however your sheet writes dates (05/04/2030, 4-May-2030, 2030-05-04). A past date lands as a card that's due — that's the point. An unreadable one goes to staff review.

specialty.detail: Deep, wreck, night, or drysuit. One cell can name several (“Deep, Wreck”) and each becomes its own card under the diver's agency number.

nitrox.detail: A yes/no column, plus the nitrox card number if you keep one — that's what brings it across.

rentalSizes.detail: BCD, wetsuit, boot, and fin — whatever sizes you track become a fit profile.

pastVisits.detail: A date, trip name, and price per row becomes that diver's history here, so a regular arrives as a regular. Repeat their email on each row to match the right person.

cutover.heading: Cutover without drama
cutover.intro: Leaving a system you've run for years doesn't have to mean a weekend of downtime. Here's the switch, step by step.

step1.title: Run both systems for one trip cycle
step1.detail: Import into DiveDay and start taking real trips through it — waivers, roster, manifest — while you keep your old system running alongside it. Nothing forces a hard cutoff on day one.

step2.title: Time it to your slow season
step2.detail: Pick a week with the fewest trips already on the books. Fewer live bookings straddling the switch means less to reconcile by hand.

step3.title: A second import updates your roster, it doesn't duplicate it
step3.detail: Re-run the export later, once your old system has more bookings in it. DiveDay matches existing divers by email and updates them instead of creating a second record, and a repeated visit history collapses instead of doubling.

step4.title: Budget an afternoon, not a week
step4.detail: Exporting from the old system is minutes of work, and the preview shows exactly what will land before anything saves. Review it, fix any flagged rows, import for real. One sitting, not a project plan.

item1.title: Readiness that won't let an unready diver board
item1.detail: The trip and the dive site decide what each diver needs; if a card or waiver can't be verified, DiveDay says so plainly instead of passing them through. {competitor} takes the booking — it never checks whether the diver is cleared to get on the boat.

item2.title: Certification checks that actually gate the dive
item2.detail: DiveDay gates the dive on the card: a deep dive won't clear a diver who isn't carded for it, and every nitrox fill is re-checked at fill time. Cards you enter are verified by staff; cards you bring in come across verified and flagged imported, with a one-tap confirm.

item3.title: Native waivers with medical review — in every tier
item3.detail: Waivers are built in and versioned against your own release, and a medical answer that calls for a physician's sign-off blocks the diver until that review — it doesn't just warn. Not a form stapled to a checkout, and not a paid add-on.

item4.title: A roll-call manifest that survives the dock
item4.detail: Big Boarded / Not-boarded buttons for wet thumbs, a head count for every dive, and a manifest the crew saves to the phone so it keeps working after the signal drops at the ramp.

item5.title: Rental fit and the trip's packing list
item5.detail: Every diver's sizes become the boat's kit list, with a tank per diver per dive split by air and nitrox. {competitor} doesn't know a diver's wetsuit size.

item6.title: The night-before brief and a recap they share
item6.detail: Each diver gets a plain-language brief the night before — dock time, conditions, what to bring — and a shareable recap page after. The booking confirmation was the start; this is the rest of the relationship.

contact.detail: Imported as given. A row with an email matches an existing diver on re-import; without one, it's always a new record.

emergencyContact.detail: Name and phone carry over when present.

diveInsurance.detail: Carried across as free text, exactly as your file holds it. Never a gate — just detail the crew wants on hand.

rentalSizes.detail: BCD, wetsuit, boot, and fin sizes become a rental-fit profile.

certificationCard.detail: Imported verified and flagged imported, refresher date included — staff give it a one-tap confirm; unrecognized levels need manual entry.

specialtyCards.detail: Imported as verified specialty cards, flagged imported; each one still needs a staff confirm before the dive that requires it.

nitrox.detail: Imported as a verified nitrox card, flagged imported — but a diver gets plain air until staff confirm it; boarding never waits.

signedWaivers.detail: A row marked already-accepted is trusted, medical clearance included, and marked imported — individual medical answers are never reconstructed, only the outcome.

waiverDocuments.detail: Fetched once from your file's URL and re-stored in DiveDay's own storage for audit. Images and PDFs up to 5 MB.

role.detail: Everyone imports as a diver. Staff roles and logins are never granted by import.

cardOnFile.detail: Stays with your payment processor — DiveDay never imports card or payment data.

pastVisits.detail: One row per booking becomes visit history — not a dive, and it never appears on your schedule or counts toward capacity.

receiptsService.detail: Payment records stay with your processor; gear-service history has nowhere to land — DiveDay tracks sizes, not individual rigs.

eve.cardSummary: Long the Windows desktop shop-management system for PADI retailers, now owned by DiveShop360. Export your customers and cards, then bring them here.
eve.metaDescription: Leaving EVE? A step-by-step guide to exporting your customers and certifications from EVE and bringing them into DiveDay — what comes across, what doesn't, and why.
eve.heroLede: EVE keeps your divers and their cards on a Windows PC in the back office. Here's how to get that data out of EVE yourself and bring your people, cards, and rental sizes into DiveDay — with a plain account of what makes the trip and what stays behind.

context.item1: EVE (from Integrated Scuba Systems) is the desktop shop-management system PADI retailers ran for years, and DiveShop360 acquired it in 2023. If you're planning a move off it, this guide is about the practical part: getting your people and their cards out of EVE and into DiveDay.
context.item2: The part that makes leaving feel risky is real: EVE stores its data in a database on your own PC, and shops report that years of purchase and service history are hard to pull out cleanly. DiveDay's import isn't trying to move all that. It moves what you need on day one — your roster, their certification cards, their rental sizes — so your people are trip-ready from the first booking, and the history stays where it already is.
context.item3: One rule we won't bend: you export your own file from your own EVE install. DiveDay never logs into EVE and never reaches across to another system to pull your data — that's your data to hand us, not ours to take.

eve.exportHeading: Get your data out of EVE
eve.exportIntro: EVE runs on Windows, so this happens on the back-office PC where it's installed, not on a website. The goal is a spreadsheet of your customers and their certification cards. Menu labels shifted across EVE versions, so treat these as the shape of the path, not word-for-word buttons.

step1.title: Open EVE on the shop PC and sign in with a manager account
step1.detail: Reporting and exports live in the back office, behind a manager or owner login — not the point-of-sale till. Use the PC where EVE actually holds its database.

step2.title: Open the customer list or a customer/certification report
step2.detail: Find the area that lists every customer with their certification details — usually under a Customers or Reports menu. You want the full roster, not a single record.

step3.title: Widen the range to all customers, all time
step3.detail: If the list or report asks for a date range or an active-only filter, set it as broad as it goes so recent-only or lapsed customers aren't quietly left out.

step4.title: Export to Excel or CSV and save it
step4.detail: EVE's lists and reports export to a spreadsheet — choose CSV if it's offered, or export to Excel and use File → Save As → CSV. Save it somewhere you'll find it, like the desktop.

step5.title: Do the same for certifications if they're a separate report
step5.detail: If cards (agency, level, card number) live in their own report rather than on the customer list, export that too. A card number is what lets DiveDay bring a card across at all.

step6.title: Can't reach the export? Ask EVE's current owner
step6.detail: If your license has lapsed or the export is greyed out, DiveShop360 now owns EVE and can produce a customer and certification export for you. Ask in writing and keep the file — that file is all DiveDay needs.

exportNotes.note1: Do this while your EVE install still opens and your license is active — a working export today beats chasing it later.
exportNotes.note2: Your column headings don't have to match anything. DiveDay recognizes the common names EVE and every other system use, and shows you exactly how each column mapped before you commit.
exportNotes.note3: If EVE will give you a sales or booking report as well, take it — a file with one row per booking brings your regulars' visit history across, so a fifteen-year customer doesn't arrive looking brand new. Register receipts and repair tickets stay in EVE; see the scope table below.

diveshop360.cardSummary: The retail-POS incumbent. Export the customer and certification CSVs its own FAQ names, then bring your people across.
diveshop360.metaDescription: Leaving DiveShop360? A step-by-step guide to exporting your customers and certification data as CSV and bringing them into DiveDay — what comes across, what doesn't, and why.
diveshop360.heroLede: DiveShop360 keeps your customers and their cards in the cloud, and its own help pages name the datasets you can export as CSV. Here's how to pull your people and certifications and bring them into DiveDay — with a plain account of what makes the trip and what stays behind.

context.item1: DiveShop360 grew out of a retail point-of-sale system, and that's where it's strongest — registers, inventory, vendor catalogs. Its own FAQ names four CSV exports: customers, inventory, sales reports, and certification data. A move to DiveDay needs two of them — customers and certification data.
context.item2: We're not here to replace your point of sale. DiveDay runs the water — bookings, readiness, the boat — so “bring your POS, we run the dive day” is a real division of labor, not a slogan. That's why we only ask for the customer and certification files.
context.item3: One rule we won't bend: you export your own CSV from your own DiveShop360 account. DiveDay never signs into DiveShop360 and never reaches across to pull your data — that's your data to hand us, not ours to take.

diveshop360.exportHeading: Get your data out of DiveShop360
diveshop360.exportIntro: DiveShop360 runs in a browser, and exports come from the back-office admin, not the register. You want two CSVs — customers and certification data. There's no public API or bulk export, so it's a manual, dataset-by-dataset download, and menu labels shift between versions.

step1.title: Sign into DiveShop360 admin as an owner or manager
step1.detail: Exports live in the back office, behind an owner or manager login — not the point-of-sale screen your front desk rings sales on.

step2.title: Find the customer export
step2.detail: Look under Customers or Reports for a CSV export of your customer list. DiveShop360's own FAQ lists customers as one of the four datasets you can export.

step3.title: Export all customers to CSV
step3.detail: Export the whole customer list, not a filtered or single-page view, so no one is left behind. Save the file where you'll find it.

step4.title: Export the certification data too
step4.detail: Certifications are a separate one of DiveShop360's four exportable datasets. Export it as CSV — it holds the agency, level, and card number, and the card number is what lets a card come across at all.

step5.title: Skip inventory and sales reports
step5.detail: Those are the other two exportable datasets. You don't need them for DiveDay — we're not your POS. Keep them for your own records.

step6.title: Stuck on an export? Ask DiveShop360 support
step6.detail: If a dataset won't export from the UI, their support can produce a customer or certification CSV. Ask in writing and keep the file — that file is all DiveDay needs.

exportNotes.note1: Manual CSV, dataset by dataset, is a limit of DiveShop360 — no API, no bulk export, no webhooks — not of DiveDay. Doing it yourself from the admin is the whole path.
exportNotes.note2: Your column headings don't have to match anything. DiveDay recognizes the common names DiveShop360 and every other system use, and shows you exactly how each column mapped before you commit.
exportNotes.note3: If you can also export a booking or sales report, bring it — one row per booking becomes your divers' visit history here. Retail receipts, repair tickets, and your e-commerce site stay in DiveShop360; see the scope table below.

diveshop360.importerNote: DiveShop360 exports customers and certification data as two separate files. Import the customer file first — DiveDay matches people by email, so the certification file adds to the same divers instead of duplicating them. That file usually holds one row per card: a diver with three cards appears on three rows, each landing on that one diver, and a row reading “PADI Deep Diver” becomes a deep specialty card.

smartwaiver.cardSummary: Export your participant CSV and bring the people across — a waiver your file already shows as signed comes in marked imported, so nobody has to sign twice.
smartwaiver.metaDescription: Moving off Smartwaiver? A step-by-step guide to exporting your participants and bringing them, and their already-signed waivers, into DiveDay.
smartwaiver.heroLede: Smartwaiver holds signed waivers and the people who signed them, exportable as a participant CSV. Here's how to bring those people — and, where your file shows a waiver already accepted, that acceptance too — into DiveDay, where waivers are native and versioned against your own template.

context.item1: Smartwaiver does one thing — digital waivers — and some shops reach it because their booking system (DiveShop360 among them) outsources waivers to it. DiveDay's waivers are native and in every tier, so moving off means bringing the people across and telling DiveDay which of them already have a waiver on file.
context.item2: The people migrate cleanly: a Smartwaiver participant export carries names, email, phone, and often an emergency contact — the roster you need. What it doesn't hold is certification cards or rental sizes; a waiver system isn't where those live.
context.item3: If a row in your export marks a diver's waiver as already accepted, DiveDay's importer trusts that and brings the waiver across too — marked imported, dated to the acceptance date in your file, and satisfying the boarding gate without asking the diver to sign again. It isn't a copy of the signed Smartwaiver PDF itself (that stays in Smartwaiver, or you can attach a saved copy of it during import); it's your prior acceptance, carried forward.
context.item4: One rule we won't bend: you export your own participant CSV from your own Smartwaiver account. DiveDay never signs into Smartwaiver and never reaches across to pull your data — that's your data to hand us, not ours to take.

smartwaiver.exportHeading: Get your data out of Smartwaiver
smartwaiver.exportIntro: Smartwaiver runs in a browser. The goal is a participant CSV — the people who signed your waivers. Menu labels shift over time, so treat these as the shape of the path, not word-for-word buttons.

step1.title: Sign into your Smartwaiver dashboard
step1.detail: Exports live in the dashboard, behind your account login.

step2.title: Open the waiver or participant search
step2.detail: Find the area that lists the people who have signed — usually a waivers or participants search with an export option.

step3.title: Set the date range wide, then export to CSV
step3.detail: Set the range as broad as it goes — all time — so every participant is included, then export the list to CSV and save it where you'll find it.

step4.title: That CSV is your roster
step4.detail: Names, email, phone, and any emergency contact you collected are what come across, along with whichever column in your export shows a waiver as already signed — if it has one.

exportNotes.note1: Smartwaiver holds waivers, not certification cards or gear sizes — so mostly it's the people who migrate, and that's the roster you need.
exportNotes.note2: Your column headings don't have to match anything. DiveDay recognizes the common names Smartwaiver and every other system use, and shows you exactly how each column mapped before you commit.
exportNotes.note3: A diver your file shows as already signed comes across marked imported, not asked to sign again — see the scope table below for exactly what that does and doesn't carry over.

smartwaiver.importerNote: A Smartwaiver export is mostly contact data — expect people and emergency contacts to import, and no certification cards or rental sizes (a waiver system doesn't hold them). A waiver your export shows as already accepted comes across too, marked imported.

context.item1: FareHarbor is an online booking platform for tours, activities, and rentals — owned by Booking Holdings, the company behind Booking.com — and plenty of dive shops run their storefront on it. It's good at that job: guests book and pay online, and its distribution network puts your trips in front of hotels, concierges, and resellers you'd never reach on your own.
context.item2: What it isn't is dive software. FareHarbor makes no claim to certification gating, medical waivers that fail closed, rental-gear fit, or a boat manifest built for a roll call — it's a general booking engine, not a dive shop's back office. Its “manifest” is a passenger list you can download; it has no concept of a C-card.
context.item3: And the storefront isn't free: FareHarbor charges nothing monthly, but takes a fee on every booking — added to your guest's checkout price — for as long as you use it. It doesn't publish the rate; you hear it on a sales call (third parties report around 6%). A cut of every booking, forever, is what a growing shop feels.

step5.detail: FareHarbor has an API, but access is partner-gated — you email their support to request it, and it's built for resellers, not a self-serve export you can run yourself. The Dashboard CSV is your route out, and it's enough.

about.heroTitle: Your season doesn't hang on us.
about.phoneFrameLabel: A captain running roll call in DiveDay from the phone's offline copy.
about.heroDescription: Payments run through your own Stripe account, your records download as one ZIP any day, and roll call works on a phone with no signal. Divers build DiveDay — and everything below is either something you can go and try in the next few minutes, or something we're telling you outright that we don't do.
about.founderP1: A dive shop owner walked me through an ordinary day: a whiteboard, a clipboard, a hand-updated spreadsheet, and a few apps that don't talk to each other. He was paying for it twice — once in software, again in the hours it pulled from his divers.
about.founderP2: That's the pattern: an entire industry running on software nobody built for it — dated at best, hostile at worst, built for a back office, not a wet dock. Shops keep the whiteboard and clipboard because paper never crashes, never logs you out, never needs five taps with wet hands.
about.founderP3: DiveDay closes that gap: software fast, clear, and forgiving enough that a crew reaches for it unprompted — built from watching how a boat day runs, not a spec written far from the water. If your team wouldn't open it on a busy morning, it hasn't done its job.
about.runP1: Write in about a bad morning at the counter, a bug, or a question — a real person reads it and helps, not a form that asks you to attach a screenshot before anyone looks.
about.runP2: Pricing works the same way: the whole of it is on one page, and you can read every line of it without talking to anyone here first.
about.rulesTitle: Four rules, and you can check every one.
about.rulesDescription: These aren't promises. Each one is something you can go and prove wrong in the demo, in about a minute.

survivesDock.title: It has to survive the dock.
survivesDock.body: Wet hands, bright sun, one bar of signal, a boat that's already late. If a screen only works sitting down in an office, it hasn't been finished.
survivesDock.check: save a manifest to your phone, turn the network off, and run roll call anyway.

noSilentPasses.title: No silent passes.
noSilentPasses.body: Software that quietly waves a diver through because a field was blank is worse than paper. When DiveDay can't verify something, it says so and stops — and says which thing.
noSilentPasses.check: open the blockers queue and read why each name is on it.

onePrice.title: One price, no seats.
onePrice.body: Everything the product does is in the price. There is no tier that hides the feature you actually need, and nobody here is paid to sell you more of it.
onePrice.check: read the pricing page. It's one number and one list.

yourRecords.title: Your records are yours.
yourRecords.body: The export isn't a retention lever we release when you threaten to leave. It's a button, it works on day one of a trial, and it hands back documented files rather than a proprietary dump.
yourRecords.check: start a trial and download the ZIP before you've entered anything.

about.plainlyTitle: What we're not going to pretend.
about.plainlyDescription: You'd find these out anyway. Better now than after you've moved a season of bookings.

new.title: DiveDay is new.
new.body: You'd be among the first shops on it. That's why the demo is a working shop instead of a sales call, and why the export button works on your first day.

notEverything.title: It doesn't do everything.
notEverything.body: No retail register, no agency sync, no gear inventory. Those are real jobs done by other software, and pretending otherwise would only waste a season of yours.

stillMoving.title: It's still moving.
stillMoving.body: Shops that join now steer what gets built next — what your crew hits this season is what gets attention. The trade is a product that bends toward your shop while it's still changing under you.

about.leaveP1: These are the records that get your divers on a boat, so here's what's worth knowing before you hand them over — starting with the part that decides it, which is how you'd take them back.
about.leaveP2: {terms} Coming the other way, a person will sit with your old export or spreadsheet and bring your divers across with you.
about.whereLiveValue: On servers in the United States, in a download you can take at any time, and — if you want a second copy somewhere we can't reach — in a weekly delivery to storage your shop owns.
about.committingValue: Month to month, per location, cancel whenever. No setup fee, no contract to get out of.
about.whoAnswersValue: A real person on the DiveDay team — email {email} anytime.
about.closingTitle: The honest way to judge all of this is to go use it.
about.closingDescription: No call, no form first. Walk a full sample shop as the owner, the captain, or a diver, and decide whether it feels like something your crew would open on a busy morning.

product.pricedBody: Payment is part of the same readiness answer as the waiver and the card. Nobody boards on an assumption that someone else already settled up.

pricing.heroDescription: No setup fee. No per-seat math. No feature tiers. No cut of your bookings.

feeAnchor.title: A flat price, or a cut of every seat you sell.
feeAnchor.body: Two of the booking channels a dive shop gets offered charge by the booking instead of by the month. Here is what each says about its own price — not what any shop ends up paying, which we won't guess.
feeAnchor.rezdy: {competitor}'s current published pricing is a monthly subscription plus 3% of every online booking. The option with no monthly fee still takes the 3%.
feeAnchor.fareharbor: {competitor} publishes no rate at all. It charges nothing monthly and takes a fee on every booking, added to your guest's checkout price, for as long as you use it; third parties report that fee at around 6%.
feeAnchor.ours: DiveDay takes no cut of a booking. Checkout runs through your own Stripe account, and what you pay us is the price above — the same number in a busy August as in a quiet January.
feeAnchor.sourcesNote: Both descriptions come from the switching guides, where each one is cited to the incumbent's own pages.

dataExit.title: The exit is a button, not a support ticket.
dataExit.body: Every diver, booking, signed waiver and payment history, as documented CSVs — plus every photo the shop stored, as real files rather than links. One ZIP, downloaded by the shop's owner from Settings, on any day including the first day of a trial.
dataExit.honestNote: Two things it will not hand over, and the screen says so: login accounts with their password hashes, and the push credentials tied to a particular phone. Neither means anything in another system, and a file of password hashes is not something a download button should produce.

pricing.faqTitle: The questions that actually decide it.

billing.question: How does billing work?
billing.answer: Month to month, per location. Cancel whenever you like and leave with your shop's records through the export button — no setup fee and no annual contract.

trialMeaning.question: What does "trial" mean right now?
trialMeaning.answer: Starting a shop is free for 3 weeks, no card required — and nothing switches off when the window ends; what you set up keeps working. When you're ready to move to paid, email {email}.

seeBefore.question: Can I see it before I commit?
seeBefore.answer: Yes. The live demo is a shop already full of sample trips — walk the day as the owner, an instructor, a divemaster, the captain, or a diver. A trial shop of your own starts empty, ready for your first trip.

offline.question: Does the manifest work offline?
offline.answer: Yes. The crew saves the manifest to their phone before leaving the dock. Departure and after-dive roll calls work from that copy, the screen always shows how fresh it is, and when service returns DiveDay checks every change against the live manifest before it counts.

dataIfNotWorking.question: What happens to my records if I leave?
dataIfNotWorking.answer: You leave with your shop's records, whenever you choose. {claim} {terms}

switching.question: What does switching to DiveDay actually involve?
switching.answer: Export a spreadsheet of customers from your current system, and DiveDay's importer brings in your divers, cards, and rental sizes — showing exactly what will happen before anything is saved. Step-by-step guides cover {competitors}.

agency.question: Does DiveDay connect to PADI or SSI?
agency.answer: No agency lets software verify a C-card automatically, so DiveDay doesn't pretend. A photo goes on the diver's profile once; staff confirm it with the agency, and it stays with them for good. Courses arrive as your shop's copy of the agency catalog — you set prices and visibility.

pos.question: Does DiveDay replace my POS?
pos.answer: No — keep your register. DiveDay runs the water side: bookings, courses, readiness, prep, and the boat, paid through your own Stripe account. Add a retail line to an order, but there's no register or stock count here.

whyFounding.question: Why be a founding shop?
whyFounding.answer: Because early shops steer — what your crew runs into shapes what ships next. Founding shops also lock in today's price for two years, and every new feature lands in the one plan there is, with no higher tiers to move things into.

multipleLocations.question: What about multiple locations?
multipleLocations.answer: Each DiveDay shop runs one location today. If you operate more than one location, email {email} — we'd rather build that with you than pretend it's already here.
